newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian euthanasia patients in last ditch plea.
newsitem.headline: Australian euthanasia patients in last ditch plea.

text.p: Despondent Australian pro-euthanasia activists made a last ditch plea on Tuesday to delay the quashing of the world's first euthanasia law so two terminally ill people could kill themselves legally.
The Australian upper house of parliament voted 38 to 33 in the early hours of Tuesday to reject the law that Northern Territory passed last year to allow terminally ill people to commit suicide.
The anti-euthanasia bill, which had already been passed by the lower house of parliament, needs to be rubber-stamped by Governor-General William Deane to become law.

Leading euthanasia campaigner Doctor Phillip Nitschke, who has helped four people die under the law, said two people would write to the governor-general pleading for him to delay his signature so they can kill themselves legally.
"The patients will be asking for that in a statement to the governor-general today," Nitschke told Reuters. "They would ask for there to be some delay, perhaps for a week or two," he said.
A dejected Nitschke said he was disgusted by the efforts of those supporting the anti-euthanasia bill in the Senate to try to accelerate the bill's signing into law.
"The same callous disregard that was being shown last night is being demonstrated, in the sense that they're now calling on the governor-general to sign it as fast as possible," he said.

Four people have legally killed themselves, using a computer-controlled machine that injects a lethal drug, since the territory's legislation came into effect in July. The first was 66-year-old cancer sufferer Bob Dent, who used it in September to end what he called "a roller-coaster of pain".
Euthanasia has remained illegal in the rest of Australia but supporters and opponents agree that it is widely practised.

Nitschke said it was too late for the two patients to kill themselves legally unless there was a delay in signing the bill into law. He would not say whether the patients would take their own lives regardless of the quashing of the law.
Anti-euthanasia activists congratulated the Senate on its early-morning vote.

"While we feel a deep sense of compassion for those who are suffering and longing for release from pain, we must recognise that the Senate vote shows that there is still a sense of reverence for life in our community," Sydney Anglican Archbishop Harry Goodhew said in a statement.
"The taking of a person's life is contrary to God's law and the values of civilised society and I am deeply thankful that the Senate agrees," he said.
Argument in the heated debate continued to rage over the nation's airwaves on talk-back radio shows the morning after the vote.
"It's just so sad that our personal decisions have taken away by arrogant politicians. It's personal choice isn't it?" said Rhonda, a caller to a Sydney radio station.
Robert, a terminally ill cancer patient, rang to say he was happy the euthanasia law had been rejected.

"I'm totally opposed to euthanasia because it involves bringing in a third person on your self-destruction. That's the most abhorrent, contemptible thing that you can do," he said, his voice shaking with emotion.
